scenes.text: Here's someone who's had asthma since they were six. They train four days a week, they carry a reliever puffer to every game, and they know exactly what sets their chest off. Ask them about their health and they'll say, "I'm healthy." A doctor reading their file might not agree. So who's right? To answer that, we need to know what health actually means, and why people define it so differently.

Health is what's called a contested idea. That means sensible people disagree about where its edges are. The definition you'll meet most often comes from the World Health Organization. It says health is "a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity." It's been part of the organisation's constitution since that came into force in 1948, and the wording hasn't changed since.

Two phrases do most of the work. "Not merely the absence of disease" makes health something you have, not just a gap where illness isn't. Older medical ideas worked the other way round, so anyone without a diagnosis counted as healthy by default. And "physical, mental and social" brings three dimensions inside health. So someone with no disease, but no sleep, no friends and nowhere secure to live, isn't healthy on this definition. That's why governments quote it. It lets them treat housing and loneliness as health problems.

Now underline the word "complete". It's where the main criticism lands. If health means complete wellbeing in all three dimensions, then on a strict reading almost nobody is healthy at any given moment. And it's harsh on people living with a chronic condition or a disability, like our athlete with asthma, who'd count as unhealthy for life. But that doesn't make the definition useless. It was written as an aim for health systems, a statement of what they should work towards, not a test for sorting people into healthy and unhealthy.

The WHO definition isn't the only meaning in use, and the others aren't just worse versions of it. Two are narrower. The biomedical meaning says health is the absence of diagnosable disease or injury. It's precise and testable, which is exactly what a doctor needs at three in the morning, but it says almost nothing about whether a life is going well. Under it, our athlete isn't healthy. The functional meaning says health is being able to do what your life asks of you. Under that one, they clearly are.

One meaning is wider than the WHO's. The holistic meaning sees the whole person in their whole context, not a body on its own. In Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander health, this idea is called social and emotional wellbeing. It covers connection to body, to mind and emotions, to family and kinship, community, culture, Country, and spirituality and ancestors. And it treats a person's health and their community's health as one thing, not two separate topics.

Line the four meanings up from narrowest to widest, and a pattern appears. Every time you widen a definition, it becomes more relevant to real lives, but less precise. Every time you narrow it, it becomes more precise, but less relevant. The biomedical meaning can be settled with a lab test and tells you little about a life. The holistic meaning describes a life well, but it's very hard to turn into a number.

So why do people choose different meanings? It isn't random. People tend to define health by what health has cost or given them. A sixteen-year-old often means energy and fitness, while an eighty-year-old means getting to the shops on their own. Living with a condition moves people from "nothing wrong" to "managing it well". Culture sets whether health belongs to one body or to a family and community. A labourer needs a different body from an accountant. And people with fewer resources often set the bar where they can actually reach it. None of these is wrong. Each meaning is situated: built by someone, somewhere, for a purpose.

When a question says compare, don't describe one meaning and then the other, and don't just pick a winner. Put them side by side on the same three questions. What does each one count? What does it leave out? And whose work does it make possible? Try it on our athlete. Biomedical counts the diagnosis, so it calls them unwell. Functional counts what they can do, so it calls them healthy. Biomedical leaves out how their life is going, while functional has no fixed line. One serves the doctor, the other serves the person. Neither is wrong. They're built for different jobs.
Two lines to remember. Widening a meaning buys relevance and costs precision. And to compare any two meanings, ask what each one counts, what it leaves out, and who it's useful for.

Two exam questions. First. A doctor finds no disease and tells a patient that no treatment is needed. A council health officer says the same patient's overcrowded housing is a health problem. Identify the meaning of health each person is using, and explain how both of them can be correct. Pause here to answer.

The doctor is using the biomedical meaning: no diagnosable disease, so no treatment. The council officer is using the WHO definition, which counts social wellbeing, so housing becomes a health matter. Both can be correct, because each definition is built for a different job. The classic mistake is deciding that one of them must be wrong.
Second. Compare the WHO definition of health with the biomedical meaning of health. Pause here to answer.

Shared ground first: both treat disease as relevant, and the WHO includes it with "not merely". Then run the three questions. Biomedical counts only disease, while the WHO adds mental and social wellbeing. Biomedical leaves out how a life is going, while "complete" leaves out almost everyone. The classic mistake is two separate paragraphs that never meet.

So, when you meet any definition of health, don't ask whether it's right. Ask what it counts, what it leaves out, and whose work it makes possible. Next, we'll take the three dimensions inside the WHO definition, and see how a change in one of them spreads to the others.
